source_text: Καὶ πᾶσί γε τούτοις ἐπιλέγει ὁ Κέλσου Ἰουδαῖος· ταῦτα μὲν οὖν ὑμῖν ἐκ τῶν ὑμετέρων συγγραμμάτων, ἐφ᾿ οἷς οὐδενὸς ἄλλου μάρτυρος χρῄζομεν· αὐτοὶ γὰρ ἑαυτοῖς περιπίπτετε, ἠλέγξαμεν δ᾿ ὅτι παρὰ τὰ ἡμέτερα τῶν εὐαγγελίων συγγράμματα πολλὰ πεφλυάρηται ἐν τοῖς τοῦ Ἰουδαίου εἴτε πρὸς τὸν Ἰησοῦν εἴτε πρὸς ἡμᾶς λόγοις. καὶ οὐχ ἡγοῦμαί γε ὅτι παρέστησε, πῶς ἡμεῖς ἑαυτοῖς περιπίπτομεν, ἀλλὰ μόνον οἴεται, ἐπεὶ δὲ προστίθησι τούτοις ὁ Ἰουδαῖος αὐτοῦ ὅτι ὅλως, ὦ ὕψιστε καὶ οὐράνιε, τίς θεὸς παρὼν εἰς ἀνθρώπους ἀπιστεῖται; λεκτέον πρὸς αὐτὸν ὅτι καὶ κατὰ τὸν Μωϋσέως νόμον θεὸς ἐναργέστατα παραγεγονέναι τοῖς Ἑβραίοις ἀναγεγραμμένος οὐ μόνον κατὰ τὰ ἐν Αἰγύπτῳ σημεῖα καὶ τέρατα ἔτι δὲ τὴν δίοδον τῆς ἐρυθρᾶς θαλάσσης καὶ τὸν στῦλον „τοῦ πυρὸς“ καὶ τὴν νεφέλην τοῦ φωτὸς, ἀλλὰ καὶ ἡνίκα ἡ δεκάλογος ὅλῳ τῷ λαῷ ἀπηγγέλλετο, ἠπιστήθη ὑπὸ τῶν εἰδότων· οὐκ ἂν γὰρ, πιστεύοντες τῷ ἑωραμένῳ καὶ ἀκουσθέντι, μόσχον κατεσκεύα σαν οὐδ᾿ „ἠλλάξαντο ἂν τὴν δόξαν ἑαυτῶν ἐν ὁμοιώματι μόσχου ἐσθίοντος χόρτον“ οὐδ᾿ ἔλεγον ἂν πρὸς ἀλλήλους περὶ τοῦ μόσχου· „οὗτοί εἰσιν οἱ θεοί σου, Ἰσραὴλ, οἵτινες ἀνήγαγόν (σε) ἐκ γῆς Αἰγύπτου.“ καὶ ὅρα εἰ μὴ κατὰ τοὺς αὐτούς ἐστι τηλικούτοις τεραστίοις καὶ τοσαύταις ἐπιφανείαις θεοῦ καὶ πρότερον ἀπιστῆσαι δι᾿ ὅλης τῆς ἐρήμου, ὡς ἐν τῷ νόμῳ Ἰουδαίων γέγραπται, καὶ κατὰ τὴν Ἰησοῦ παράδοξον ἐπιδημίαν μὴ ἁλῶναι ὑπὸ τῶν μετ᾿ ἐξουσίας αὐτῷ εἰρημένων λόγων καὶ τῶν παραδόξως αὐτῷ ἐν ὄψει παντὸς τοῦ λαοῦ πεπραγμένων.
pass_a_gloss: And upon all these things the Jew of Celsus adds (ἐπιλέγω): 'These things then [we have put] to you from your own writings (σύγγραμμα), for which we need (χρῄζω) no other witness (μάρτυς); for you yourselves fall foul of (περιπίπτω) yourselves.' But we proved (ἐλέγχω) that contrary to (παρά + acc.) our writings of the gospels many things have been babbled (φλυαρέω) in the words of the Jew whether toward Jesus or toward us. And I do not think that he showed (παρίστημι) how we fall foul of ourselves, but only he thinks [so]. And since his Jew adds to these that: 'Altogether/in short (ὅλως), O most high (ὕψιστος) and heavenly (οὐράνιος) one, what god (θεός) being present (πάρειμι) among (εἰς) men is disbelieved (ἀπιστέω)?', it must be said (λεκτέον) to him that also according to the law (νόμος) of Moses God, recorded to have come to be present (παραγίγνομαι) most clearly (ἐναργέστατα) to the Hebrews, not only according to the signs (σημεῖον) and wonders (τέρας) in Egypt, and further the passage-through (δίοδος) of the Red Sea (ἐρυθρὰ θάλασσα) and the pillar (στῦλος) 'of the fire' and the cloud (νεφέλη) of the light, but also when the decalogue (δεκάλογος) was announced (ἀπαγγέλλω) to the whole people (λαός), was disbelieved by those knowing (οἶδα). For they would not, believing (πιστεύω) the thing seen and heard, have constructed (κατασκευάζω) a calf (μόσχος), nor 'would they have exchanged (ἀλλάσσω) their glory (δόξα) in a likeness (ὁμοίωμα) of a calf eating grass (χόρτος),' nor would they say to one another about the calf: 'These are your gods (θεοί), Israel, who led you up (ἀνάγω) from land of Egypt.' And see whether it is not according to the same [people] both, with such great wonders (τεράστιον) and so many manifestations (ἐπιφάνεια) of God, earlier to disbelieve through the whole desert (ἔρημος), as has been written in the law of Jews, and at the paradoxical/extraordinary (παράδοξος) sojourn (ἐπιδημία) of Jesus not to be captured/won (ἁλίσκομαι) by the words said by him with authority (μετ' ἐξουσίας) and the things done by him extraordinarily (παραδόξως) in sight (ὄψις) of all the people.
pass_b_english: To all this Celsus’s Jew adds: “These points, then, we have drawn for you from your own writings, and for them we need no other witness; for you contradict yourselves.” But we have shown that, in conflict with our writings, the Gospels, much nonsense has been talked in the Jew’s speeches, whether addressed to Jesus or to us. And I do not think he has proved how we contradict ourselves; he only thinks so.

And since his Jew adds to this, “In short, O most high and heavenly one, what god, when present among men, is disbelieved?”, we must say to him that even according to the law of Moses God is recorded to have been most clearly present with the Hebrews, not only in the signs and wonders in Egypt (Exodus 7:3), and further in the crossing of the Red Sea (Exodus 14:21–29) and the pillar “of fire” and the cloud of light (Exodus 13:21–22), but also when the Ten Commandments were proclaimed to the whole people (Exodus 20:1–17; Deuteronomy 5:4–22); and yet he was disbelieved by those who knew these things. For if they had believed what was seen and heard, they would not have made a calf (Exodus 32:1–6), nor “exchanged their glory for the likeness of a calf that eats grass” (Psalm 106:20), nor said to one another about the calf, “These are your gods, O Israel, who brought you up out of the land of Egypt” (Exodus 32:4).

And consider whether it is not in keeping with the same people both to have disbelieved, long ago, such great marvels and so many manifestations of God throughout the whole wilderness, as is written in the law of the Jews, and, at the extraordinary coming of Jesus, not to be won over by the words he spoke with authority (compare Matthew 7:29) and by the marvels he did in the sight of all the people.

choices.why: 'whether against Jesus or against us' made 'whether addressed to Jesus or to us' (πρός marks the addressee: the Jew speaks to Jesus, then to Jewish believers)

translator_notes: Celsus’s words are marked: the Jew’s summing-up (‘These points... you contradict yourselves’) and the mocking question ‘In short, O most high and heavenly one, what god... is disbelieved?’ ‘god’ is lowercase there because Celsus speaks of a god in general; ‘God’ is capitalised where Origen means the God of Israel. ταῦτα μὲν οὖν ὑμῖν ἐκ τῶν ὑμετέρων συγγραμμάτων has no verb; ‘we have drawn for you’ supplies the sense. περιπίπτετε ἑαυτοῖς (‘you fall foul of yourselves’) rendered ‘you contradict yourselves’, and the same in Origen’s reply. εἴτε πρὸς τὸν Ἰησοῦν εἴτε πρὸς ἡμᾶς is rendered ‘whether addressed to Jesus or to us’: Celsus’s Jew first speaks to Jesus himself and then to Jewish believers, so πρός marks the addressee here, not hostility. Psalm 106:20 is LXX Psalm 105:20 (ἠλλάξαντο τὴν δόξαν αὐτῶν ἐν ὁμοιώματι μόσχου ἔσθοντος χόρτον); Origen has ἑαυτῶν and ἐσθίοντος; ‘calf’ follows the LXX μόσχος (the Hebrew has ‘ox’). ‘These are your gods, O Israel...’ is Exodus 32:4 (repeated at 32:8); σε is a supplement in the staged text, kept. The staged text splits κατεσκεύασαν across a space; read as one word. ‘Signs and wonders in Egypt’ is cited at Exodus 7:3, where the phrase is used; the plagues themselves run Exodus 7-12. ‘The cloud of light’ is taken as the pillar of cloud of Exodus 13:21-22. Disbelief ‘throughout the whole wilderness’ recalls passages such as Numbers 14:11 and Psalm 78 (LXX 77); not cited inline because no single text is quoted. ‘With authority’ echoes Matthew 7:29 (ὡς ἐξουσίαν ἔχων), marked ‘compare’.
